performers: Berlin Philharmonic Orchestra; Wilhelm Furtwängler, conductor
intro: Furtwängler and the Berlin Philharmonic play Tchaikovsky’s slow finale, recorded in Berlin in 1938. Its falling violin melody passes from one section to the other before the music sinks to the double basses’ low B.

sections.label: A · The divided violin melody
sections.mNote: First and second violins exchange notes of the lament

sections.label: B · The broad D-major tune
sections.mNote: A descending string melody grows above the horns

sections.label: C · The opening lament returns
sections.mNote: The strings recover their B-minor melody

sections.label: D · Strings and brass press on
sections.mNote: The returning lament expands towards its final climax

sections.label: E · F♯ and the low brass
sections.mNote: The dominant subsides towards the quiet brass chorale

sections.label: Coda · The last B-minor descent
sections.mNote: The second tune returns above the basses’ low B

cues.title: A tune shared between desks
cues.text: The first and second violins pass the falling melody between them, one note at a time. Each section’s part looks broken on the page. Together they sing a continuous line above the opening half-diminished chord.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 16, reproduces the violin parts. Opening harmony: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky). https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The composer’s private ending
cues.text: In February 1893 Tchaikovsky writes to Vladimir Davydov about his planned finale: “a long drawn-out adagio”. He is delighted with the new symphony, whose programme he intends to keep secret.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Vladimir Davydov, letter 4865, 11/23 February 1893. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6

cues.title: Horns beneath the song
cues.text: The Andante brings a broad melody in D major. First violins and violas sing above the horns, and trombones answer them. Even this warmer tune moves downwards.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 17, describes the Andante scoring; D-major key at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Back to B minor
cues.text: The opening lament returns in the strings. Tchaikovsky stretches its falling phrases across the orchestra, building again from the melody that began the movement.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 17, describes the opening theme’s return and expansion. https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The lament fills the orchestra
cues.text: Strings and brass carry the returning lament towards its last climax. F♯, the dominant of B minor, holds beneath the agitated melody before the music begins its long withdrawal.
cues.evidence: Finale’s late climax and F♯ pedal: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky); Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 17.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Pride after the première
cues.text: On 30 October 1893, two days after conducting the première in Saint Petersburg, Tchaikovsky writes to his publisher Jurgenson. The symphony has caused bewilderment, he says, but “I’m more proud of it than any of my other works”.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Pyotr Jurgenson, letter 5062, 18/30 October 1893. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6

cues.title: Low B beneath the strings
cues.text: The last return of the broad melody is in B minor. Muted strings descend above the double basses’ repeated low B. The closing pages leave more and more of the music to the cellos and basses.
cues.evidence: Final return in B minor and muted strings: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky). Low-B pulse and thinning close: https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: He could make a ballroom glitter, then let one unguarded melody tell us who was unhappy there.
facts: School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck: an allowance, 1877–90, and a friendship conducted by letter
Three ballets; Eugene Onegin, The Queen of Spades and other operas
composer.background:
At Kamenka on 6 July 1878, Tchaikovsky was explaining to Nadezhda von Meck how he composed. Ideas arrived in the middle of conversations; he held them in his head until he could sketch them on the first sheet of paper that came to hand. Waiting for the right mood was no way to work. “Inspiration is a guest who does not like to visit the idle,” he told her. Then he broke off for dinner. At two o’clock he resumed, moving on to sketching, orchestration, fair copies and how far a symphony must keep to its traditional form. Here is the composer of extravagant passions in his own voice: observant, companionable, exact about his trade.

He was born in Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. He grew deeply attached to his French governess, Fanny Dürbach, and began piano lessons at the end of 1845. The profession chosen for him was the law. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg. Four years later his mother died of cholera. He graduated in 1859 and took a post at the Ministry of Justice, while opera and concerts increasingly claimed his attention.
